text: Every chapter so far has been about getting an environment running: network, compute, storage, monitoring, backup. All of that work is real and necessary. But a deployment that only works correctly because one person remembers how it's all wired together isn't actually finished — it's fragile in a way that doesn't show up until that person is unavailable, and by then it's too late to fix cheaply.

Picture a small team's cloud environment, built over a few weeks by one engineer, with every decision about subnets, NSG rules, and backup schedules living only in their head. It runs fine for months. Then that engineer takes a two-week vacation, and a security rule breaks a vendor integration on day three. Nobody else on the team knows which rule to touch, why it was set up that way, or what else might break if they change it — a twenty-minute fix becomes two days of cautious trial and error.

The difference is rarely the configuration itself — it's whether anyone wrote down why. The same network security group can ship with no context at all, or with a short comment block above it: its purpose, the ticket that justified the rule, and who owns it. Same resource, same rules, identical behavior in production, but only one version tells the next engineer anything useful when they're staring at it during a live incident at 2 a.m.

That's why this course treats documentation as part of a deployment's definition of 'done,' not an optional extra tacked on afterward if time allows. Deployed means the resources exist and run. Tested means a smoke test confirms they actually work end to end. Documented means someone other than the person who built it could understand it and operate it safely. An environment only counts as finished once it clears all three bars, not just the first two.

A useful gut check is the six-month test: if the builder vanished for six months, could a teammate answer why a subnet is sized the way it is, or where the backup job's logs land, without guessing or reverse-engineering the whole setup? If the honest answer is no, that's documentation debt sitting quietly in production, and it gets collected during an incident, under pressure, at the worst possible time.
